subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: I live next door, so I hear it all. Naveen, two, has Hindi from his father, Punjabi from his Dadi and English from picture books. This morning he pointed at the kitchen and said, "Dadi, paani, water more!" Later he shouted, "Roti, please, chahiye!" His mother laughed and gave him the glass. I can't tell what he understands of each language, but he knows every word gets him what he wants. Dadi says he will sort them out later. Minakshi

qa.q: Which languages does Naveen hear at home?
qa.a: Naveen hears Hindi from his father, Punjabi from his Dadi and English from picture books.

qa.q: What might Naveen be feeling when he says "Dadi, paani, water more!"?
qa.a: Naveen wants water and is happily using every word he knows to get it. He seems eager, not confused.

qa.q: What choice did Naveen's mother make when he mixed the words?
qa.a: She laughed and gave him the glass, treating the mixed words as normal talk and not correcting him.

qa.q: What does Dadi think will happen to Naveen's mixing of languages?
qa.a: Dadi thinks he will sort the languages out later, which fits how toddlers gradually separate the sounds they hear.

grounding: A toddler in a home with Hindi, Punjabi and English mixes words from all of them, which is normal, and the child will sort them out with time.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Monday. Ujjwal, two, pointed at the moon. "Chanda... moon!" At home they speak Hindi and Punjabi, and nursery sings in English. Amandeep smiled. Wednesday. "Doodh! More milk!" Ujjwal said, holding out the cup. Amandeep filled it. Saturday. Ujjwal told his Nani "moon" and told his Nana "chanda", pointing at the sky each time, checking who understood.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal point at on Monday?
qa.a: Ujjwal pointed at the moon.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling or wanting when he says "moon" to Nani and "chanda" to Nana?
qa.a: Ujjwal is trying words out and checking who understands, with curiosity and pleasure, not confusion.

qa.q: What choice did Amandeep make when Ujjwal mixed the words, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Amandeep smiled and filled the cup without correcting, which lets Ujjwal keep exploring the sounds and words from all the languages.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Ujjwal said "moon" to her?
qa.a: Probably delighted, since the toddler was sharing a word and looking for a reply from her.

grounding: A toddler in a home speaking Hindi, Punjabi and English mixes words from all of them, which is normal, and gradually sorts them out.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
In the Bengaluru flat, Nitin, two, pointed at the ceiling fan. "Fan! Ghoom-ghoom!" Then, to his Thatha Shankar: "Thatha, beda!" when Thatha tried to switch it off.
Amma laughed. "Kannada, Hindi and English, all in one breath."
Thatha frowned. "Won't he get confused?"
"He's sorting," Amma said.
Nitin tugged Thatha's hand, said "Come, come," and led him to the window to see the birds.

qa.q: What did Nitin point at?
qa.a: Nitin pointed at the ceiling fan.

qa.q: What might Thatha have been worried about when he frowned?
qa.a: Thatha was worried that mixing three languages would confuse Nitin.

qa.q: What could Amma tell Thatha to reassure him?
qa.a: She could explain, as she began to, that mixing words is normal for a toddler sorting sounds, and that Nitin will separate the languages with time.

qa.q: How might Nitin experience his three languages?
qa.a: To Nitin they are all just words for the things and people he loves, so he uses whichever comes first.

grounding: A toddler in a home with Kannada, Hindi and English mixes words from all three, and a parent sees it as normal sorting.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
"Papa, doodh!"
"Milk? Here you go, Siddharth."
"Mo-o-re dudh!"
"More milk? Okay."
"Papa, kukur!" Siddharth pointed at the street dog.
Tushar laughed. "Kukur in Bangla, kutta in Hindi, dog in English. You've got all three, little man."
Nani, visiting, shook her head. "He should stick to one, na?"
"He will, Ma. He's two. His brain is sorting."
Siddharth waved at the dog. "Bye, doggy! Bye, kukur!"

qa.q: What did Siddharth point at?
qa.a: Siddharth pointed at the street dog.

qa.q: How might Nani be feeling when she shakes her head?
qa.a: Nani seems worried that learning several languages at once is too much for Siddharth.

qa.q: How does Tushar handle Nani's worry well?
qa.a: He calmly explains that Siddharth is two and his brain is sorting, reassuring her that mixing is normal.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth to have three words for one thing?
qa.a: For Siddharth it seems fun and natural; he happily uses all of them to talk about what he sees.

grounding: A toddler hearing Bangla, Hindi and English mixes all three, and a parent explains this is normal and healthy sorting.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
Daycare note, toddler room, Wednesday.
At snack time Pranav, two and a half, he said, "Mera biscuit, mine!" and then, in Marathi, asked for water. He called the ball "chendu."
His father, Nitin, asked at pickup if we were worried: Dadi speaks Marathi, they speak Hindi, daycare is English. I told him mixing is common and healthy at this age.
Next step: we asked the family to keep speaking their own languages at home.

qa.q: What did Pranav call the ball?
qa.a: He called the ball "chendu."

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he asked if the daycare was worried?
qa.a: Nitin was probably anxious that the language mixing meant something was wrong.

qa.q: Why did the caregiver ask the family to keep speaking their own languages?
qa.a: Keeping each language rich at home helps Pranav, whose mixing is normal and healthy, sort out all three over time.

qa.q: How might Pranav's Dadi benefit from the caregiver's advice?
qa.a: Dadi can keep talking to Pranav in Marathi, staying close to him in her own language.

grounding: A daycare note shows a toddler mixing Hindi, Marathi and English, reassuring a parent that this is normal and healthy.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: In the courtyard of their house in Satara, Jaya, just two, held up her empty cup to Aaji. "More doodh, please! Pani nako!" Aaji laughed and poured milk. Rukmini, her mother, heard it from the well: Hindi, Marathi and English in one breath. A neighbour frowned. "She'll get confused." Rukmini shook her head. "She's sorting it out." Jaya pointed at the hen. "Kombdi! Chicken!" and toddled after it, calling both words at once.

qa.q: What did Jaya ask Aaji for?
qa.a: Jaya asked Aaji for more doodh.

qa.q: What does Jaya's toddling after the hen suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She seems excited and happy, delighting in the hen and in naming it with both words.

qa.q: What was wise about Rukmini's reply to the neighbour?
qa.a: Rukmini calmly treated the mixing as normal sorting, not confusion, so Jaya can keep enjoying all her languages.

qa.q: Why might the neighbour see Jaya's mixing differently?
qa.a: The neighbour worries three languages will confuse her, not seeing that small children mix words while they learn to separate them.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a multilingual home mixing words from three languages as a normal, healthy part of sorting sounds.
